I grabbed the Link and Controller a few months ago. Honestly, I'm not a fan of Steam and wasn't expecting to care for the Link since I'd streamed to my TV previously using a laptop and found it clunky. The Link is not clunky. It's awesome.

I love my Steam Link and use it almost daily. It really is a great device although it has some caveats. First off, you really need a wired connection (it supports WiFi, but it isn't optimal). I use a powerline adapter with mine and it's great. Next, I am just not good enough with controllers to do well with FPSs so I've been sticking to genres that lend themselves to more laid-back gaming...basically stuff like platformers, adventure games, walking-sims...shit that doesn't require quick reflexes or precision aiming. That said, the Link supports keyboard & mouse and I've used mine on Doom and it works fine...it's just not comfortable (for me) to use the k&m in my living room.

The Steam Controller is good, but takes a LOT of getting used to--and even then you might not love it. It is highly customizable and theoretically you should be able to play any game with one. You can use a PS4 controller with the Link or a wired XBox One controller (and apparently controllers from older console generations as well). Still, if you're going to buy a Link, I highly recommend just getting the Steam Controller as well. It is worth it.

Steam has been putting these on sale a few times recently, but the sale price is always $35. The combo deal is a good deal ($63 for both). If you're on the fence, I recommend you grab a set. I can't imagine they'll ever sell them for cheaper than $31.50 apiece. If I can answer any questions before you buy, I'm happy to do so.

I have both.

Steam Controller is very nice, but has a bit of a learning curve and the amount of options can be a bit daunting. It also isn't really plug and play, it does work that way, but you really need to learn how to set it up properly and how to use the insane amount of options it has to get the most out of it.

It will probably feel weird and awkward to use at first, but if you stick it out and learn how to handle it properly, it's the best PC gamepad on the market, and especially nice to have with Steam Link. The only problem is that getting used to it takes a bit and it doesn't feel right at first, and it can take a week or two of regular use to start really getting comfortable with it and figure out how to tweak the settings properly for individual games.

Steam Link is the best part of the deal though. Worth every penny, especially since it can also be used to run your desktop from whatever you have it hooked up to. Use it more for streaming video more than I do gaming. Plus, it natively connects to the Xbox 1, Wii U Pro, and Dual Shock 4 controllers wirelessly, which is nice.

It's really great for doing PC stuff on a television in general, not just gaming. At least get a wireless mouse to go with it though, and having a wireless keyboard is a good idea too. You don't have to use them for gaming from the couch as that can be a bit awkward, but they are a lot better for navigating the desktop and doing internet stuff. You can set up the desktop controls to emulate a mouse with a controller, but it's not nearly as good.

Would not part with either, but if I absolutely had to choose just one, I'd keep my Steam Link.

Just to clarify what /u/Contrabardus is talking about--the Link allows you to minimize Steam's Big Picture Mode and just drop you to your PC's desktop. While in this mode, you can completely control your PC remotely. The Steam Controller provides a mouse cursor, but you can easily use a real keyboard & mouse through the Link for full desktop access. It's like a VNC client...it's a handy feature to have and one that isn't advertised or discussed much (although the feature isn't hidden at all).

As I mentioned in an earlier reply--the Steam Controller really has people split. Some folks really LOVE how flexible it is, but others feel it presents too high of a learning curve. I'm pretty sure Valve is going to release an updated Controller in 2017 but don't let that dissuade you from buying one now (at these prices). Even if you already have a controller that works with the Link, the Steam Controller is worth having. I bought my Link without the controller initially and after a couple of weeks I went ahead and ordered one despite my concerns--I'm glad I did.

I have to offer a counterpoint to the Steam Link. I have a wired connection to it, I upgraded my graphics card for it, I use shadow play, for a couple of weeks it worked butter smooth playing shadow of mordor on high-ultra settings at 1080p at a high framerate... worked perfect...

Then there was a patch, it became unplayable, every 1-2 minutes there's 10-20 seconds video freeze (Sound still happens) it also runs slow as hell now and has a very low framerate.

Nothing in my hardware or connection has changed, all that changed was an update, and now I can't even play the simplest indie games at 360p without it shitting all over the place.

Just a buyer-beware, people have different experiences with the Steam Link, it may work for you, it may not.... it might work for you and then just stop working...

I've read about folks having similar experiences to what you've mentioned although I've never read that a Link just quit working. The "complaint" I've heard most is that updates to the Link can greatly impact certain games. What I have yet to come across is a number of people validating that a specific game is negatively affected...for example an update rolls out and Doom quits working. I don't discount the claims as I've seen them on and off. What folks should know--the Link offers you a setting to run the Stable firmware or Beta firmware. There are a lot of internet posts dating back to 2015 (when the Link was released) advising people to run the Beta as there were some more serious bugs when the device was first released. I ran the Beta myself, but when I experienced some sync issues, I switched back to the Stable channel and have been fine since. There are a lot of factors that could affect your experience, not the least of which is your network connection. As mentioned in my OP, the Link supports wireless, but it is NOT recommended. You NEED a wired connection to play most games. I use a powerline adapter and although that works well for me, I know there are some inherent limitations to it versus running some Cat 5 cable through my house.

I'd recommend folks go read reviews for the Link over at Amazon, but read the most recent ones. Steam didn't have the software fully baked when it was first released in 2015 so reviews from then don't really reflect the current state of the device. Reviews of the Steam Controller are all over the map because it really is a polarizing device--there are a lot of traditional console controller users who really hate the Steam Controller. As someone who isn't a console gamer (but who owns an XBox One), I am can see why folks are frustrated but still appreciate some of the unique features. I initially ordered the Link without the controller but after using a k&m and an Xbox One controller for awhile I went ahead and got the Steam Controller. I'm glad I did--it is a better experience with the native controller.

Bottom line: I don't really recommend the Link/Controller when they're not on sale (normal price is $50 each/$100 for both). But at $63 for both it's well worth the gamble that you'll really like it. You might experience some issues here and there, but Steam does provide a Stable and Beta channel and has a number of streaming settings you can tweak to optimize performance. Of course, like /u/Pattoe mentions, YMMV, but overall the devices have good ratings and can provide a lot of flexibility for gaming at a very modest price.

If anyone is wondering, the Steam controller alone is 30% off by itself, sans combo. I just built an htpc capable of running steam games natively, so I was interested in this without the link combo deal, and was surprised to find the controller at such a bargain by itself.
